item.title: SpaceX to launch solar arrays and 6,300 pounds of cargo to the ISS
item.description:
NASA and SpaceX are set to launch new solar arrays and 6,300 pounds of cargo to the International Space Station aboard the CRS-35 mission, lifting off Tuesday at 6:33 a.m. EDT from Cape Canaveral. The research manifest focuses on human and plant health plus drug-resistant organisms — the kind of applied science the station does best.

It's a fitting capstone to a busy day for SpaceX, which also launched 27 Starlink satellites from California on Monday evening.

Sources

item.title: Antarctic sea ice reaches third-lowest maximum on record
item.description:
Antarctic sea ice grew to its 2026 maximum — and it's the third-lowest maximum extent since satellite observations began. The southern ice story remains the concerning one: the Arctic gets the headlines, but Antarctica's shrinking winter maximums are the trend to watch.

Sources

  • NASA: Antarctic Sea Ice Grows to Its 2026 Maximum

item.title: APOD: ice fishing for cosmic neutrinos
item.description:
Today's Astronomy Picture of the Day goes to the South Pole — 'ice fishing' for cosmic neutrinos with detectors buried in Antarctic ice.

A beautiful reminder that some of the universe's most elusive particles are caught not with telescopes, but with a cubic kilometer of ice and a lot of patience.

Sources

  • NASA: APOD: 2026 October 11 – Ice Fishing for Cosmic Neutrinos

item.title: NASA flyover and fan events at MetLife Stadium
item.description:
NASA announced a flyover plus fan-engagement events at MetLife Stadium, bringing the space agency's outreach directly to an NFL audience.

It's part of a broader, ongoing push to meet the public where they already are rather than expecting them to come to NASA. Sports tie-ins have become one of the agency's favorite outreach channels.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA to Conduct Flyover, Engage NFL Fans at MetLife Stadium

item.title: Astronomy Picture of the Day: the lunar farside
item.description:
Today's Astronomy Picture of the Day showcases the lunar farside — the hemisphere of the Moon permanently turned away from Earth — in striking detail.

It's a reminder of how much of our nearest neighbor we never see from the ground, and why farside missions remain scientifically compelling.
